summary: Cranberry Island Light, off Cape Canso at the east entrance to the Strait of Canso, was first shown in 1818 (or 1815, per NSLPS); the present light dates from 1929 or 1978.

structures.note: Earlier octagonal tower with red and white stripes; construction began 1817 (LF; NS Archives), first lit 1818 (LF) or 1815 (NSLPS). Two fixed lights in 1858 (LF). Burned in 1881 (LF) or 1883 (NSLPS).
Temporary fifty-foot skeleton tower with two lights from 8 November 1881 (LF).
Octagonal tower, red and white bands, with a dwelling attached; LF gives 78 ft (23.8 m); NSLPS table gives 60 ft for the 1883 tower. Replaced in 1929 (NSLPS).
NSLPS: square concrete tower, white with red lantern, 1929. LF: a new tower attached to the fog-alarm building in 1929, a square concrete-block tower in 1978. The accounts do not match.
Steel skeleton tower with an enclosed central stair (LF); moved to Jeddore Rock in 1978 (LF).
Square concrete-block tower attached to a rectangular concrete building (LF only).
LF: a light on a square skeletal tower stands beside the lighthouse. CCG: square skeleton tower, red and white rectangular daymark. The sources do not say which structure carries the light today.
New fog alarm on the summit of the southern part of the island, with a diaphone; square wooden building, sides white and roof red (Department report).

access.note: NSLPS: site access by boat. LF: 2.7 km offshore. Owned by the Canadian Coast Guard.

events.note: Construction began in 1817 (LF: work from 1 June to 19 October, continued the next summer). NS Archives holds construction documents of 1817.
Put into operation 1 November 1818 (LF). NSLPS gives 1815 for the earlier tower. See resolved_conflicts.
Duty at harbours adjacent to the Gut of Canso set up to support the light; continued by an act of 1827 (8 Geo. IV, c. 12).
Daboll fog trumpets put in operation 20 September 1865 (LF). NSLPS gives a fog signal in 1864, which it calls the province's first.
Fog trumpet disabled 30 August 1870 and discontinued until a steam whistle could be installed (LF).
Steam whistle placed in charge of John Cormack, $450 a year, from 9 September 1871 (LF).
Great Nova Scotia Cyclone, 24 August 1873: sea over the island, boats and coal carried off, upper light out from 10 p.m. until daylight (LF, quoting the Department's report).

Fire on 13 October 1881 (LF) destroyed the new tower and dwelling, except the oil store and storehouse; lighting apparatus lost. A Wilmington newspaper of 15 October 1881 says 'yesterday morning' (14 October). NSLPS gives 1883 for the fire.
Two temporary lights shown from a fifty-foot skeleton tower on 8 November 1881 (LF).
Salvaged fog alarm machinery overhauled in Halifax and placed in operation 1 July 1882 (LF).
Octagonal tower and attached dwelling, contract $3,690 to John G. Sinclair of Country Harbour, due by end of June 1883 (LF). NSLPS dates the octagonal tower to 1883.
Third-order Fresnel lens by Chance Brothers for a fixed white light; sixth-order light in a bay window 35 ft below (LF).
Neptune fog trumpet replaced the steam fog whistle (LF).
Diaphone fog alarm put in operation 1 July 1906, one blast of seven seconds each minute (Department report for the year to June 1906; LF).
Dwelling for the fog alarm engineer, contract $2,200 (Department report for the year to June 1908).
Upper light changed from fixed white to occulting white, 3 s visible, 5 s eclipsed, 17 s visible, 5 s eclipsed, in 30 s (Department report for the year to June 1910; LF).
Lower light discontinued (Department report for the year to June 1910; LF).
NSLPS dates the diaphone fog signal to 1911; the Department report dates the diaphone to 1906. See notes.
Steamer Imperoyal stranded on Grimes Rock near Cranberry Island, 15 June 1923; got off, escorted to Halifax, drydocked.
New tower attached to the fog-alarm building; old light discontinued (LF). NSLPS: present square concrete tower begun 1929.
Two-storey double dwelling added; head keeper and two assistants (LF).
Steel skeleton tower erected and electronic horn replaced the diaphone; one assistant's post eliminated (LF).
Square concrete-block tower built; skeleton tower moved to Jeddore Rock (LF only).
Submarine cable laid to connect the station to commercial electricity (LF).
The island's single dwelling torn down (LF).
Station de-staffed in 1986 (LF); NSLPS: automated by 1986.
Boathouse removed after being declared surplus (LF).
Electric lantern, flashing white 15 s, with fog signal (NSLPS).

wrecks.outcome: Stranded on Grimes Rock near Cranberry Island at 3.25 a.m. The Arras, then at Canso, was asked to help, but the Imperoyal got off first; the Arras escorted her to Halifax, where she was placed in drydock.

corrections.why: 1929 is the date of the present tower, not of the first light. LF gives first light 1 November 1818; NSLPS gives 1815 for the earlier tower; the 1817 construction documents fit LF's account. Record: Rowlett's 'Year of the tower described' mislabels 1929 as first lit.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The CCG list (entry 668) and NSLPS (Cranberry Islands III, 'Operating: This light is operational') both show the light active. The record's Rowlett 'inactive' is not supported.

The record's 1929 is the present tower (LF; NSLPS). LF's first light is 1818 and NSLPS's earlier tower is 1815; this record uses 1818 because the 1817 construction documents and LF's account of the building work fit that year better.
Lighthouse Friends gives the fire of 13 October 1881, and the Wilmington paper of 15 October 1881 fits that date. NSLPS gives 1883 ('destroyed by fire'). The story gives 1881 and notes NSLPS's 1883.
Lighthouse Friends gives 78 ft (23.8 m) for the 1883 octagonal tower; NSLPS's table gives 60 ft (18.3 m). The story gives both figures.

notes_for_editor: First light is unresolved: LF gives 1 November 1818 (with 1817 construction papers at the NS Archives and an 1822 duty act that supported the light); NSLPS gives 1815 for its earlier tower and names an engineer, 'Patrick Lannegan', where LF has keeper 'Patrick Lanigan'. The record's 1929 was the present tower, not the first light. The first fog signal: NSLPS 1864 ('NS's first') against LF's 1865 (Daboll trumpets, 20 September 1865); pre-1900 Department reports are not in the local corpus, so this cannot be checked here. The 1881 fire: LF gives 13 October 1881; the Wilmington paper of 15 October says 'yesterday morning' (14 October); NSLPS says 1883. The 1883 tower height: LF 78 ft; NSLPS table 60 ft. The diaphone: the Department report for the year to June 1906 gives operation from 1 July 1906 (primary); NSLPS says 1911. The present tower: NSLPS gives 1929; LF gives a 1929 tower and a 1978 concrete-block tower, and a skeletal light tower beside the lighthouse; CCG describes a square skeleton tower with a daymark. The sources do not say which structure carries the light. James P. Hanlon: LF gives him for 1854-1883 and again for 1905-1914; the Department lists a Hanlon at Cranberry in 1905-06; the sources do not say whether one man. The 1873 cyclone details are from LF's quotation of the Department's report; the report itself is outside the corpus (which starts in 1900). Of the eleven roster lines, nine rest on LF alone; the Sullivan (1902 list) and 1905-06 Hanlon (1906 list) lines are also in the Department's lists, read from a single row each. All named keepers ended their service before 1960. Not searched: a Chronicling America search for the 1873 cyclone at Cranberry Island; the 1929 and 1978 tower dates have no independent source here. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the Sullivan row (1902 list, scan 245, printed 68) and the Hanlon row (1906 list, scan 181, printed 172) were checked on the page image. Sullivan reads Cape Canso, Cranberry Island, L. H. & F. W. | May 23, 1887 | 800.00. Hanlon reads Cranberry Island Light and Fog Alarm with its appointment cell blank and salary 800.00. The lower-light discontinuance (scan 94, printed 94) was confirmed on the scan. The Imperoyal stranding (15 June 1923) is in the Department's 1923-24 report, but that date falls in fiscal 1922-23; the wreck list appears to run by navigation season, so the story gives the report without a fiscal-year reading of the event. The report calls the Arras 'C.G.S.'; the story calls it a government ship, not a Coast Guard vessel.
